transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-21 14:00 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Anika (RE), Jenna (CTO, Astra), Leo (SRE), Priya (ML Eng), Tom (Infra)

Summary (auto): p95/p99 tail analysis across streaming vs non-streaming, KV cache behavior, batching strategies, quantization impact, and network hop contributions. Agreed to run empirical benchmarks with Astra's prompt set; deliverables: perf CSV and follow-up.

Topics: p99 sources, streaming chunking overhead, network RTT and multicast hops, KV cache warmup/eviction, per-batch latency vs throughput, int8/int4 quant tradeoffs, VPC egress and private deployments.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: alright everyone thanks for joining, let's kick off. we scheduled 55 minutes, main goal is to pinpoint p95 and p99 causes and propose mitigations — both config and infra.
[00:08] Jenna: yep thanks, we saw spikes during peak that push p99 to ~1.3s onshort completions which is busting our SLOs, and we want to understand whether it's model, runtime, or network.
[00:16] Carlos: quick clarification — is that 1.3s end-to-end from client SDK call to first token, or to final token?
[00:22] Leo: that's time-to-first-token, so the tail is especially bad for short responses.
[00:27] Carlos: okay makes sense. short responses amplify fixed overheads. two immediate suspects: scheduling/queuing at the inference node (batching delays), and network hops, especially in your VPC egress path.
[00:36] Priya: we saw the p50 around 90ms, p95 ~240ms, p99 1.3s  — so it's a long tail not explained by average.
[00:44] Anika: want to make sure we cover streaming vs non-streaming because we noticed different tails. streaming seems to improve first-token p50 but sometimes increases p99 due to chunking?
[00:52] Carlos: yup, streaming reduces time-to-first-token by starting generation early but adds periodic flush overheads — if the network or client stalls on the second chunk you see elongation. also gRPC vs HTTP/1 chunking behavior matters.
[01:01] Tom: our infra path includes an ALB, a NAT gateway, and a peered infra hop to the model cluster in a different AZ. could that add jitter?
[01:07] Carlos: absolutely. NAT + multiple AZ hops introduce jitter and occasional retransmits. TCP slow-start shouldn't be significant for short flows, but connection reuse and HTTP/2 multiplexing impact tail — if connection pooling isn't used you pay TLS handshake + cold TCP.
[01:18] Maya: quick note: Redwood's hosted path does connection pooling and keeps warm connections inside our runtime; for private deployments you can mirror that but sometimes customers have short-lived client instances which breaks pooling.
[01:27] Jenna: we do have ephemeral Lambdas calling the API, so pooling is spotty. can you quantify how much that contributes?
[01:33] Carlos: ballpark of cold handshake is 50-120ms depending on RTT and TLS CPU. but your p99 at 1.3s suggests there's another big contributor. we usually instrument kernel scheduling, GPU queue stalls, and KV cache misses for that.
[01:44] Priya: can you explain KV cache miss behavior clearly — our prompt set is often a shared prefix across rights, and we assumed KV hits would eliminate most compute.
[01:50] Carlos: of course. KV cache saves decoding cost for prefix tokens by reusing KV states. misses happen if the prefix wasn't seen recently on that specific serving shard or if the cache evicted entries due to memory pressure or TTL. eviction can be LRU-based and if your request fanout touches different model variants or shards you get miss-induced recomputation. miss penalty is per-token compute plus KV rewarm overhead.
[02:05] Leo: what about warm vs cold start for KV? does it store in GPU memory or host?
[02:08] Carlos: Redwood's runtime keeps active KV in GPU or pinned host memory depending on capacity. moving from host to GPU has a small memcpy cost and sometimes causes a brief scheduling pause. if the model uses 16k context, restoring KVs can be tens to a few hundred ms depending on size and memcpy bandwidth.
[02:21] Anika: and quantization — you guys recommend int8 for some models; what is impact on tail?
[02:25] Carlos: quant reduces compute and memory bandwith so it usually reduces mean and tail CPU/GPU time, but model-specific kernel implementations matter. int4 kernels can be optimized but sometimes introduce more cache thrash on attention kernels leading to jitter. overall we often see 10-30% p99 reduction with quant, but need to bench.
[02:39] Jenna: streaming vs non-streaming — we're currently using non-streaming for transactional UX. switching to streaming is non-trivial on client. is streaming safe for tail improvement?
[02:46] Maya: empirically streaming helps time-to-first-token; for p99 it can hurt if chunk flushes are serialized or your network is flaky. streaming changes the distribution: improves early percentiles, may increase heavy tails.
[02:57] Tom: can you talk about batching and its effect — we thought batching only hurts latency but helps throughput?
[03:02] Carlos: batching trades off queuing delay for per-token compute amortization. at low QPS batching can increase latency because runtime waits to fill a batch. but continuous batching and dynamic batch scheduling can keep small windows and therefore low median while giving throughput gains. for tails, spikes in queueing or head-of-line blocking inside the batch scheduler can produce long tails.
[03:21] Priya: our traffic shape has 60% short queries under 20 tokens and 40% long ones. is there a best practice to avoid long queries blocking short ones?
[03:28] Carlos: yes — priority queues by request size, or separate worker pools by max tokens. Redwood supports routing small-SLO requests to low-latency pools and heavy requests to throughput-optimized pools; that avoids head-of-line blocking.
[03:40] Jenna: we have a single pool today. would splitting require infra changes?
[03:43] Maya: for hosted it's config only; for dedicated/private you can set separate instance groups and autoscale policies.
[03:49] Leo: network hops again — do you have tracing to show which hop introduces jitter?
[03:52] Carlos: we use distributed tracing (span per client->edge->runtime->GPU). common issues: NAT gateway CPU throttling, egress bandwidth saturation, and cross-AZ peering high p99. we can correlate high tail requests to specific AZ/instance. for private deployments you can run perf tests pinned to a subnet to rule out egress.
[04:08] Priya: what's the typical diagnostic-run you recommend to reproduce our p99?
[04:11] Carlos: three-step: 1) replay your real traffic at scale (10-50%) across both streaming and non-streaming modes; 2) run with p95/p99 tracing enabled and KV cache metrics exported; 3) isolate cold vs hot caches by toggling TTL and measuring rewarm penalties. we provide a benchmark harness template.
[04:27] Anika: also capture connection lifetimes to catch handshake-related tails.
[04:30] Maya: one more point — model compilation during first inference (jit or kernel selection) can cause an outlier if the runtime compiles a new kernel path for a rare sequence length. we precompile common sequences for predictable workloads.
[04:42] Jenna: do compiles occur at runtime for hosted?
[04:45] Carlos: sometimes; we have background compilation and warm pools to reduce this. but if a rare sequence triggers a kernel not in cache you can see ms-to-seconds overhead.
[04:54] Priya: can you give concrete expectations — like if we enable dedicated small-pool with int8 quant and streaming, what p99 reduction might we see?
[05:00] Carlos: rough example for short-response workloads: baseline p99 1.3s. eliminate cold-handshakes and NAT jitter (-0.1s), separate small-request pool (-0.2s), KV hit-rate improvements and pinning (-0.4s), quantization benefits (-0.2s) — you could target ~400-600ms p99. actual numbers depend on KV hit rate and network topology.
[05:18] Tom: wow that's optimistic; what's the risk of introducing more complexity with multiple pools?
[05:22] Maya: operationally it's an added config but we automate routing policies. downside is cost slightly increases if you reserve low-latency capacity.
[05:28] Leo: what's the overhead of enabling per-request tracing?
[05:31] Carlos: tracing adds small CPU overhead and a few ms to latency at high sampling rates. we usually sample at 1-5% for production, or 100% in ephemeral perf runs.
[05:39] Jenna: any quick fixes we can do this week to reduce tail?
[05:42] Maya: immediate: ensure your clients reuse connections (keep-alive / HTTP2 pooling), enable streaming for first-token sensitive flows, and carve a small dedicated low-latency pool for short requests. we can push a config change and you can run a single-hour perf ramp.
[05:54] Priya: can you share the perf spreadsheet and a template for the benchmark harness?
[05:57] Maya: yes, I'll share the spreadsheet and the harness link after this call.
[06:01] Carlos: also we'll include instrumentation knobs for KV TTL, batch window, and quantization flags.
[06:06] Jenna: on security and private deployment — if we move to VPC private deployment, will network hops reduce?
[06:12] Carlos: typically yes — private VPC deployment removes public NAT and ALB egress, reducing an entire network layer. tail jitter is often much lower when everything is in-subnet. note: you'll need to manage KMS integration and audit logs; we'll share the security docs.
[06:27] Tom: any gotchas with on-prem? we have air-gapped infra sometimes.
[06:31] Maya: on-prem adds variance in kernel driver versions and NIC offload features — those can impact memcpy and RDMA performance. we recommend validated HW stack or using Redwood Dedicated where we manage the runtime.
[06:43] Priya: one more — about batching windows, you mentioned dynamic batching. can you expand?
[06:47] Carlos: dynamic batching groups requests by sequence length and arrival time; it uses a small max-wait window (e.g., 5-15ms) and adaptive thresholds to avoid growing latency at low QPS. it's better than fixed-window batching for mixed workloads.
[06:58] Jenna: if we implement these suggestions, how long to show improvement?
[07:01] Maya: we can do a 1-2 day pilot: config changes and a 1-hour ramped replay to catch p95/p99 signals. then a longer 24h run to stabilize data.
[07:09] Carlos: and we'll instrument and share traces and a CSV with p50/p95/p99 by route, AZ, and node.
[07:15] Maya: ok let's recap next steps.
[07:17] Jenna: go ahead.
[07:18] Maya: Redwood to run two benchmark runs — streaming and non-streaming — against Astra's prompt set. deliver perf CSV + trace samples by 2026-12-23. we'll include recommended config for KV TTL, batch window, and pool routing.
[07:29] Leo: Astra will send the prompt set and token length distribution by tomorrow 2026-12-22.
[07:33] Priya: we'll also test client connection pooling changes on our end.
[07:36] Maya: action items captured; follow-up scheduled week of 2026-12-28 to review results.
[07:41] Jenna: thanks everyone, this was helpful.
[07:44] Maya: thanks all, we'll send the doc and spreadsheet.

Notes and artifacts shared: perf benchmark template (link), KV metrics dashboard screenshot (link), security checklist (link).

End of transcript.
